newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU gas oil stocks likely to have risen - analysts.
newsitem.headline: EU gas oil stocks likely to have risen - analysts.

text.p: Figures due out on Tuesday are expected to show a modest build in October of European oil stocks, including those of distillates, analysts said on Monday.

They steer clear of outright predictions, but many say they believe the evidence suggests a stock build is likely following the sharp fall among the fourteen countries of the EU excluding Sweden in September.
Like one month ago, the distillate stocks figure of the Euroilstock report will be the one commanding most attention.
"The distillate number is going to be important... and the market ought to take notice," said UBS energy economist Geoff Pyne.
"The question people will ask is: was there a build in distillates, given that it was a pretty mild month?" said Mike Barry of Energy Market Consultants EMC).
Mild weather, imports of product from the United States and reduced German purchases are the key factors that should have prevented a further draw, analysts say.
"I suspect it's not going to be too exciting. (October) also tends to be a stable month," says Barry
Last month, distillate stocks dropped 2.93 million barrels, or 1.0 percent, to 283.35 million barrels, a year-on-year shortfall of 33.47 million barrels.
However, the analysts believed gas oil supply would remain short despite the likely stocks build.
"The weather of course is a big caveat, but the gas oil market will remain tight," said Lesley Owen, an analyst at Petroleum Economics.
Strong demand for distillates as domestic heating fuel at the start of the year and the continuing rise of automotive diesel demand have steadily depleted European stocks.
European demand for distillates has increased by between four and six percent this year, says Pyne of UBS.
Crude oil stocks, meanwhile, prove less contentious, but arguably less crucial to oil prices. Analysts are also less reluctant to predict the monthly change.
A modest contango of dated Brent to Brent futures and predictions of steadily rising global production in the fourth quarter suggest stocks will rise.
"My feeling is that there's probably been a reasonable crude increase," Pyne says.
Last Friday, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said that world oil demand was set to rise this winter, but that extra supplies from non-OPEC producers would help ease stock shortages.
The IEA report said global oil demand will rise to 73.8 million barrels per day (bpd) in the fourth quarter 1996, up 1.9 million year on year. However, supply is forecast to keep pace with demand.
